title: What a page may do to its window
summary: `client/manifest.json` declares the native window. It also grants (allows) the window controls that a service may use, under `tac.application.window.controls`. By default, no control is granted. A service gets the controls by injection, like the other browser APIs: `@Needs windowControls` in JavaScript and TypeScript, and a `WindowControls` field in every language that runs in the page. The calls are `granted(control)`, `minimize()`, `maximize()`, `fullscreen()`, `close()`, `resize(width, height)` and `setTitle(text)`, written in each language's case (`set_title` in Ruby, `SetTitle` in Go). A call to a control that is not granted fails at once, and the message names the grant to add. In a browser tab, `granted` answers `false` and every call fails, because the page has no native window. The host (the native app that shows the page) checks each grant again before it acts. The page has no `globalThis.tachyonWindow` global any more, and a service that reads `globalThis` fails to build with `TY1360`. Compiled Swift services in a macOS app can also request an uninitialized `WindowControls` field through `Needs` or `NeedsAll`; the activation provider calls the host directly with the same grants (ADR 0089). Rust native services use activation-owned providers too; the macOS adapter targets the app’s own window and is qualified through actual title/resize changes. The native Rust/C#/Swift/Kotlin alternatives below use Service and NeedsAll with an uninitialized typed WindowControls field. Rust targets desktop hosts, C# targets Windows, Swift targets Apple platforms and Kotlin targets Android. C#/Kotlin provider and host-registration ABI/SDK checks are recorded in ADR 0089; Windows/Android operating-system interaction has not been run on this Mac. Browser and native sources are shown as separate target alternatives; native/ is a documentation folder, and the selected native file belongs in the application’s client/services/. Native service code belongs to the application. It runs as normal operating-system code, and this window-control policy does not sandbox (limit) it.
